Your strawberry frosting containing FD&C Red No. 3 must stop being manufactured with that color additive by January 15, 2027. On that date, the removal of 21 CFR 74.303 (the listing authorizing FD&C Red No. 3 in food) takes effect, and all existing certificates for batches of FD&C Red No. 3 cease to be effective for use in food (90 FR 4628; 91 FR 50475). The administrative stay that was in place from February 18, 2025, was lifted on August 5, 2026, and the effective date of January 15, 2027, was confirmed (91 FR 50475).

Regarding product already on shelves: The January 2025 order explicitly states that '[w]hen FD&C Red No. 3 has been used in food or ingested drugs while its certificate is still effective, such food or ingested drugs will not be regarded as adulterated by reason of the use of such color additive' (90 FR 4628). This means frosting manufactured and containing FD&C Red No. 3 that was incorporated while the certificate was still effective (i.e., before January 15, 2027) is NOT adulterated and may remain on shelves and be sold after that date. Only the use of FD&C Red No. 3 after its certificate ceases to be effective (i.e., incorporating it into food on or after January 15, 2027) would render the food adulterated.

Note: The January 2025 order sets no separate compliance date; the operative deadline is derived from the effective date of January 15, 2027. There is no phase-out period beyond that date for manufacturing.

response.answer:
Under the updated 'healthy' nutrient content claim rule (89 FR 106064, codified at 21 CFR 101.65(d)), a food that does not qualify for one of the automatic exemptions (e.g., single-ingredient foods from encouraged food groups, or water/tea/coffee) must meet two main criteria to bear the 'healthy' claim:

1. **Food Group Equivalent (FGE) requirement**: The food must contain a specified amount of at least one food group equivalent from the food groups encouraged by the Dietary Guidelines (vegetables, fruits, whole grains, fat-free or low-fat dairy, lean meat/seafood/eggs/beans/peas/lentils/nuts/seeds). The specific FGE amounts vary by product category (individual food, mixed product, main dish, or meal) as set forth in 21 CFR 101.65(d)(3)(ii)–(v) and the associated tables.

2. **Nutrient-to-Limit (NTL) requirement**: The food must not exceed specified limits for added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium, based on a percentage of the Daily Value for these nutrients. These limits also vary by product category.

As stated in the background summary of the delay notice (90 FR 10592): the rule 'requires that, to bear a claim subject to the rule, individual food products, mixed products, main dishes, and meals must meet FGEs and specific limits for added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium based on a percentage of the Daily Value for these nutrients' (2025-03118, Section II). The preamble to the final rule (2024-29957) further explains that the FGE criteria ensure foods contain beneficial nutrients from nutrient-dense food groups, while the NTL criteria limit nutrients that should be consumed in moderation, together ensuring the 'healthy' claim signals a food that is 'foundational to a healthy diet.'

response.answer: The 'healthy' implied nutrient content claim is governed by 21 CFR 101.65(d). This section defines the general nutritional claims paragraph that covers labeling claims using the term 'healthy' or related terms as implied nutrient content claims because they suggest that a food may help consumers maintain healthy dietary practices due to its nutrient content. The general framework for implied nutrient content claims is set out in 21 CFR 101.13(b)(2)(ii), which defines an implied nutrient content claim as one that 'suggests that a food, because of its nutrient content, may be useful in maintaining healthy dietary practices, where there is also implied or explicit information about the nutrition content of the food (e.g., "healthy")' (passage cfr-21-101.13@2025-04-28#0000). The specific criteria for using the term 'healthy' are found in 21 CFR 101.65(d) (passages cfr-21-101.65@2024-12-01#0003 and cfr-21-101.65@2025-04-28#0003). The final rule updating the definition of 'healthy' was published at 89 FR 106064 (Doc. 2024-29957), with an effective date of April 28, 2025 (as revised by Doc. 2025-03118), and a compliance date of February 25, 2028.

response.answer: The updated 'healthy' nutrient content claim rule (Doc 2024-29957, 89 FR 106064, published 2024-12-27) does NOT apply to your dog treat product line. The rule governs the use of the term 'healthy' as an implied nutrient content claim on foods 'intended for human consumption.' Specifically, 21 CFR 101.13(a) states: 'This section and the regulations in subpart D of this part apply to foods that are intended for human consumption and that are offered for sale, including conventional foods and dietary supplements.' (cfr-21-101.13@2025-04-28#0000). Dog treats are animal food, not human food, and are therefore outside the scope of 21 CFR Part 101 entirely. Accordingly, no changes are required for your dog treat product line under this rule, regardless of whether those products bear the word 'healthy' on their labeling. Animal food labeling is governed by different regulatory frameworks (e.g., AAFCO model regulations and FDA's Center for Veterinary Medicine guidance), not by 21 CFR 101.

response.answer:
No, that was not a fair reading in mid-2025, and it is definitively incorrect now.

**What was true in mid-2025:** The January 2025 order revoking FD&C Red No. 3 (90 FR 4628, published 2025-01-16, Doc. 2025-00830) was subject to an automatic administrative stay under 21 U.S.C. 371(e)(2) as of February 18, 2025, triggered by the filing of objections. During that stay, the effective dates of January 15, 2027 (food uses, removal of 21 CFR 74.303) and January 18, 2028 (ingested drugs, removal of 21 CFR 74.1303) were suspended but not cancelled or moved. The order itself was a final binding order, not a proposal. An administrative stay does not mean a rule 'might never take effect'—it means the agency must evaluate the objections before the rule can proceed. The stated effective dates remained on the books, albeit unconfirmed during the stay period.

Saying the removal was 'not final' mischaracterized the legal posture: the January 2025 order was a final order issued under section 721(d) of the FD&C Act (90 FR 4628). The stay was a statutory procedural consequence of objections being filed, not a sign of legal infirmity or uncertainty about finality.

**What is the position now:** FDA published a document on August 5, 2026 (91 FR 50475, Doc. 2026-15920) that overrules all objections, denies requests for a public hearing, lifts the administrative stay, and explicitly confirms the effective dates of January 15, 2027, and January 18, 2028. The document states: 'we are ending the administrative stay of the January 2025 order, and under the January 2025 order we are repealing the listing for FD&C Red No. 3 in § 74.303 as a color additive in food and § 74.1303 as a color additive in ingested drugs effective January 15, 2027, and January 18, 2028, respectively' (91 FR 50475). This constitutes 'final action on the objections' under section 701(e)(2) of the FD&C Act.

The revocation is therefore fully confirmed and binding. After January 15, 2027, use of FD&C Red No. 3 in food will render such food adulterated (90 FR 4628). No compliance date is separately stated; the operative deadline is derived from the effective date of January 15, 2027 for food uses.

The Red No. 3 order (90 FR 4628, Doc. 2025-00830, published 2025-01-16) changes two CFR provisions in 21 CFR Part 74, but they do NOT all change on the same day. The amendatory instructions are as follows:

1. **Amendatory Instruction 2 – Removal of 21 CFR 74.303** (FD&C Red No. 3 for food use): This section is removed entirely, effective January 15, 2027. (2025-00830, 90 FR 4628; confirmed by 2026-15920, 91 FR 50475.)

2. **Amendatory Instruction 3 – Revision of 21 CFR 74.1303** (FD&C Red No. 3 for ingested drugs): This section is revised (to incorporate the identity and specifications previously cross-referenced from § 74.303) effective January 15, 2027, so that the ingested-drug listing remains self-contained after § 74.303 is removed. (2025-00830, 90 FR 4628, section VI.)

3. **Amendatory Instruction 4 – Removal of 21 CFR 74.1303** (FD&C Red No. 3 for ingested drugs): This section is removed entirely, effective January 18, 2028. (2025-00830, 90 FR 4628; confirmed by 2026-15920, 91 FR 50475.)

Thus, the provisions do NOT all change on the same day. Amendatory instructions 2 and 3 take effect on January 15, 2027, while amendatory instruction 4 takes effect on January 18, 2028.

The order sets no separate compliance date. Because the order is a revocation (not a new requirement to reformulate by a future date), the operative deadline is derived from the effective dates: once § 74.303 is removed on January 15, 2027, any food containing FD&C Red No. 3 is adulterated; once § 74.1303 is removed on January 18, 2028, any ingested drug containing FD&C Red No. 3 is adulterated. (2025-00830, 90 FR 4628, section VI; timeline facts.)

The order was administratively stayed under 21 U.S.C. 371(e)(2) from February 18, 2025, through August 5, 2026, but the stay has been lifted and the effective dates confirmed without change. (2026-15920, 91 FR 50475.)

response.answer: Under 21 CFR 101.65(a)(2), a 'healthy' implied nutrient content claim must be made in accordance with the general requirements for nutrient content claims in § 101.13, with one specific carve-out: § 101.13(h) is excepted when the nutrient content claim is made in accordance with paragraph (d) of § 101.65. Section 101.13(h) is the disclosure requirement that would otherwise mandate a statement such as 'See nutrition information for ___ content' when a food exceeds specified levels of fat, saturated fat, cholesterol, or sodium. This disclosure requirement does not apply to foods bearing the 'healthy' claim under § 101.65(d). All other provisions of § 101.13 — including requirements on claim type size (§ 101.13(f)), the general prohibition on nutrient content claims not made in accordance with subpart D (§ 101.13(b)), and other general principles — remain applicable to 'healthy' claims.

response.answer: Yes, your shelf-stable lentil soup labeled 'healthy' is affected by the updated definition of the term 'healthy' under the final rule published at 89 FR 106064 (Doc. 2024-29957, published 2024-12-27). This rule revises 21 CFR 101.65(d) to establish new food-group-equivalent (FGE) and nutrient-to-limit (NTL) criteria for foods bearing the 'healthy' implied nutrient content claim. Under the new framework, your lentil soup would need to qualify under one of the pathways in § 101.65(d)(3): either as a food comprised solely of qualifying ingredients with no other added ingredients except water (paragraph (d)(3)(i), which lists beans, peas, and lentils among qualifying foods), or as a mixed product meeting the FGE and NTL requirements in paragraph (d)(3)(iii). Until that compliance date, you may continue to use the 'healthy' claim under the prior criteria, but by February 25, 2028, your product must meet the updated requirements of 21 CFR 101.65(d) or remove the 'healthy' claim.

Your supplier is partially correct in a narrow technical sense but draws the wrong practical conclusion. The Red No. 3 order (Docket 2025-00830, 90 FR 4628, published 2025-01-16) indeed sets no explicit 'compliance date' — it states only effective dates. However, the absence of a compliance date does not mean there is no hard deadline. Once the effective date arrives, the listing in 21 CFR 74.303 is removed, and any food containing FD&C Red No. 3 becomes adulterated under the FD&C Act. The operative deadline is therefore derived from the effective date: January 15, 2027 for food uses (all provisions except amendatory instruction 4), and January 18, 2028 for ingested drug uses (removal of 21 CFR 74.1303). After January 15, 2027, food products colored with Red No. 3 would be adulterated regardless of when the inventory was acquired.

Important caveat: An administrative stay under 21 U.S.C. 371(e)(2) was in effect from February 18, 2025 through August 5, 2026 (per timeline source citing 2026-15920). That stay has now ended (in_force_now: false), and the stay did not change the stated dates (dates_changed: false). Therefore the January 15, 2027 effective date for food uses remains operative.

In summary: there is no stated compliance date, but there is a hard deadline — it is the effective date of January 15, 2027 for foods. After that date, the color additive listing no longer exists and products containing it are adulterated. Your supplier's conclusion that there is 'no hard deadline' is incorrect.

answer_rows.product: Any food product containing FD&C Red No. 3
answer_rows.trigger: Removal of 21 CFR 74.303 (food use listing for FD&C Red No. 3)
answer_rows.required_change: Reformulate to eliminate FD&C Red No. 3 from all food products (including dietary supplements); ensure no such products are introduced into interstate commerce after the effective date

response.answer: Your compliance memo's recorded date of January 15, 2025 is incorrect. The Red No. 3 revocation order (Document No. 2025-00830) was published in the Federal Register on January 16, 2025, at 90 FR 4628. This publication date is confirmed by both the order itself (90 FR 4628) and the subsequent order lifting the administrative stay (91 FR 50475, published August 5, 2026), which explicitly references 'the Federal Register of January 16, 2025 (90 FR 4628).' The date January 15, 2027 that appears in the document is the effective date for the food-use provisions, not the publication date. Your compliance memo should be corrected from January 15, 2025 to January 16, 2025.
